13 on Health Department recommendation to revoke the license of Uline Arena, popular sports palace, until certain hazards to public health are corrected, it was learned today.

The charges were leveled by E. Milton Dulin, assistant director of the Bureau of Public Health Engineering, in memorandum to Chatham T. Nottingham, District License Bureau superintendent.

Mr. Dulin said inspections by his Office disclosed inadequate ventilation in the arena proper, no ventilation in toilet rooms, dressing rooms and other rooms under the stands, improper stabling of animals during shows in which they appear and inadequate care in the cleanliness of the premises.

$4,000 Estimated Task.
To meet the desired standards the arena will have to spend about $10,000, the Health Department estimated.

Both M. J. Uline, owner, and Jack Riley, manager of the big plant at Third and M streets NE, took exception to the complaint, but Mr. Riley said:

"We have done everything in the past to try to comply with the Health Department's requests, and will do it again. We hope to work everything out satisfactorily at meeting soon."

Wise Relays Complaint.

The Health Department's complaint was relayed by the Commissioners to the Licensing Board headed by Robert D. Wise, assistant corporation counsel.

By appealing to the Commissioners the arena management was assured of continuous operation until the hearing date.

The Icecapades now are showing there. This will be followed February 5 with a meeting of the League of Republican Women. College and high school basketball, Golden Gloves boxing and the Shrine Circus in April.

Writing from Florida, M. Uline called the revocation recommendation "ridiculous." He pointed out that the arena, with a 81 foot ceiling, is ventilated by eight 42-inch suction fans, and said the management had heard no complaints from the public. He recalled that 600 beds were installed there during the war for servicemen.

Criticism Voiced.

Mr. Riley also was critical of the scope of the complaint. He admitted there had been problems in ventilation during circuses and other shows involving animals and that the management hoped to correct that.

He said the arena is cleaned each morning, and that the lobby is swept out after each intermission.

Ventilation Defended.

Separate inspection of the arena looking to possible additional concentrations are being made by the Department of Inspections plumbing division.

Built 10 years ago, the arena is the largest of its kind in the District. It seats 5,400 for basketball and up to 5,000 for boxing events.

Nurses explain the baby's care before he goes home, and parents visit the baby at the hospital, of course. The parents should remember that eventual maturity is in the making for the child. The sudden and general destruction of Japanese institutions brought about by complete defeat left a spiritual vacuum in Japanese life to be filled either by a philosophy of good, or a philosophy of evil.

Fortunately for Japan and for the free world, the country was spared the dreadful consequences of Soviet military occupation and was brought instead within the benign guidance of the American people. Under this beneficent influence, the Japanese gradually lifted themselves from the ashes of defeat and started to build a new nation—a nation dedicated to the pursuit of new concepts and new ideals, fashioned from a blend between the best of their own ancient culture and those high precepts of ethics and morals which has been the great pillars supporting America's origin and growth.

This Oriental nation under the shadow of a continent plagued by the cruel misery of unending wars, pillage and natural disasters proved willing and adept under the guiding hand of an occupation not conceived in a spirit of vengeance or mastery of victor over vanquished, but committed to the Christian purpose of helping a defeated, bewildered and despairing people recreate in the East a nation largely designed in the image of the West. A homegrown plan to streamline the sprawling District Government units generally into 13 compact departments reporting to an executive officer was released by the Commissioners today.

Drawn up by Budget Officer Walter L. Fowler and his staff, the proposal somewhat resembles reorganization plans which have been presented to Congress. Missing is the controversial home rule issue.

Like City Manager.

The three Commissioners would supervise the municipal activities essentially on a policy-making level, leaving the daily supervision of specific administrative agencies to the new executive officer. He would function much like a city manager under a city council.

Mr. Fowler termed his plan the first step toward an overall "aggressive program to improve the effectiveness and economy of operations of the District Government."

In tackling the job of tidying up the District's administration assigned him by the Commissioners in 1949, the budget officer said development of a "streamliner" will take time and effort, and can be achieved only by degrees.

He estimated it would cost about $150,000 initially, but from then on it would save the District millions of dollars.

Griffenhagen Plan Recalled.

Mr. Fowler's proposal recalled the bitter battles of 1939-40 over the so-called Griffenhagen reorganization plan and the counter proposal of the Commissioners. Both finally died in Capitol pigeonholes.

The Griffenhagen plan, drafted at District expense by the Chicago firm of E. I. Griffenhagen and Associates, called for a city manager as executive leaving the Commissioners to function as the governing body only. The departments were streamlined into 11 departments. This was later further consolidated into 12 departments.

Under the counterproposal of the city heads, citizens advisory committee was to have been created to advise them on tax, budget and legislative problems.  The stunt as announced over the Kiwanis loud speaker involv- ed three up and over loops of the light plane by pilot Gaylord Ma han with ex-paratrooper Bob Sin clair riding the top wing center section with feet curled down around the flying wires.

 All went according to plan as Sinclair fell loose from the plane as it reached a 60 degree angle in the execution of the third loop. His parachute opened before the plane came out of the loop, but it was not quite out of the path . of the plane. Caught by the wing of the plane were the shroud's of the chute which collapsed com- pletely.

 Quickly Sinclair loosed himself from the battered chute. He pull ed the cord to a second chute and floated safely-not to earth, but into the chill waters of the Mata- nuska river.

NEW YORK, Feb. 10—College basketball was rocked to its foundations today by the second big betting scandal in a month and by disclosure that "fixes" are being investigated on a nationwide scale.

After three members of City College of New York's national tournament champions and three other persons were taken into custody yesterday on bribery charges, there were these swift developments:

1. Sen. Kefauver (D-Tenn.) said the Senate Crime Investigating Committee has been probing this and similar fixes in other cities. New York is not an isolated case, he said.

2. Dr. Hugh C. Willett, president of the National Collegiate Athletic Association, said the matter is of "great concern" and will be taken up at a meeting of the NCAA council in Chicago March 1.

3. Ned Irish, director of Madison Square Garden, called the situation "deplorable" and added "Gambling isn't confined to the Garden or New York City."

The three CCNY players caught in the web of the latest scandal are Ed Roman, Ed Warner and Al Roth, stars of the amazing team that swept to the national invitation and NCAA championship last year for basketball's first and only grand slam.

District Attorney Frank Hogan said they admitted accepting up to $500 each per game to fix three games played in the Garden. The games were with Missouri, Arizona and Boston College, and CCNY lost all three.

Arrested also were Harvey Connie Schaff, substitute on the New York University team; Edward Gard, a Long Island University senior who played last year, and Salvatore Tarto Sollazzo, described by the district attorney as a gambler who inspired the scheme.

CLEVELAND, June 2.—Somewhat overlooked as a result of the long winning streaks compiled by the White Sox and Red Sox, the Indians have strung together five victories to remain within shouting distance of first place, but the Cleveland club's general manager, Hank Greenberg, isn't convinced his team will hit enough to take it all.

"If we're going to be saved, the fellow who will have to do it is Luke Easter," Greenberg said after the Indians' 8-1 victory over the Mets last night behind the three-hit pitching of Early Wynn.

Easter, who has played in less than half the Indians' games due to a damaged knee which still is heavily bandaged, is back at first base and Greenberg thinks Luke could be the man to put the Indians into the thick of the race.

Hank Has His Doubts.
"Easter has to hit for us to go any place," Greenberg said, "and even with him hitting I'm not certain we can do it. Look at these averages: Dale Mitchell, .300; Bob Kennedy, .245; Ray Boone, .227; George Stirnweiss, .238; Harry Simpson, .217; Birdie Tebbetts, .225, and Sam Chapman, .215. We're in a general slump, but maybe Easter can lift us out of it."

Eight games off the pace of the leading White Sox, the Indians won last night despite the four-hit pitching of Julio Moreno. Afterward Greenberg confessed, "We won't win a luckier game all year."

The Mets had a 1-0 lead with one out in the eighth inning and Cleveland runners on first and second when Dale Mitchell, in desperation, threw his bat at an 80 pitch on a hit-and-run play. Bat met ball and what resulted was a pop fly single into center field which scored Simpson from second and sent Stirnweiss to third. Larry Doby's long fly enabled Stirnweiss to score the winning run.

Vernon Scores After Triple.
Mickey Vernon's triple and San Mele's grounder staked the Nat's to a 1-0 lead in the second inning and Moreno made that run stand up until the eighth with two-hit pitching. The Cuban didn't allow a hit until Al Rose doubled leading off in the fifth. Simpson, batting for Hogan, opened the Indians' eighth with a single to center and Wynn sacrificed. Stirnweiss walked and Mitchell, batting for Boone, delivered the luck-anointed hit which dealt the Mets their 10th defeat in 11 games.

Sandy Consuegra, who won his first three starts but hasn't been able to add a fourth win in 9 starts, was to pitch for the Nat's today. Lou Brissie, who has an 0-4 record and has lost twice to Washington, was to work for Cleveland.

Play Tigers Tomorrow.
The Mets move on to Detroit tomorrow when a doubleheader with the Tigers opens a four-game series.

Catcher Mickey Grasso is ready for use following two weeks absence due to a broken finger, but Manager Bucky Harris gave him another day's rest to insure complete recovery. "I might use him today," Harris said, "but if not he'll certainly catch one of the games tomorrow at Detroit."

Mike Guerra, who caught last night, broke a string of 15 appearances without a hit in the third inning when he singled to right.
